title: Home Warranty Providers
one_liner: Home warranty providers sell service contracts that cover repair or replacement of major home systems and appliances, with demand anchored by homeownership, resale transactions and renewal pricing.
overview: Home warranty providers underwrite and administer annual residential service contracts covering normal wear-and-tear failures in systems and appliances such as HVAC, plumbing, electrical, refrigerators, dishwashers, water heaters and optional add-ons. The 2022 baseline described a mature, concentrated industry with $3.649 billion in revenue, 56 enterprises and two large operators controlling about 60.8% of revenue. By 2025, public and market sources show a larger revenue pool, with Forbes reporting U.S. home warranty provider revenue of $8.87 billion and Frontdoor alone reporting $2.093 billion of 2025 revenue after adding 2-10 HBW. Growth is now less transaction-led than in the pandemic housing boom: high mortgage rates and affordability constraints keep existing-home sales near roughly 4.0 million annualized in 2026, while renewals, price realization, contractor scale, builder warranties and non-warranty home services support revenue.

key_stats.growth: 2025 year-over-year revenue growth: 1.8%; 2020-2025 average annual growth: 3.9%
key_stats.frontdoor_2026_outlook: 2026 Frontdoor revenue outlook: $2.155 billion-$2.195 billion, up 3%-5% from 2025
key_stats.first_american_home_warranty_revenue: 2025 First American Home Warranty segment revenue: $442.9 million, up 4.0% from 2024
key_stats.frontdoor_active_warranties: 2025 Frontdoor active home warranties: approximately 2.1 million
key_stats.housing_demand_indicator: June 2026 existing-home sales: 4.09 million annualized, down 2.4% from May 2026
key_stats.profitability_indicator: Q2 2026 First American Home Warranty pretax margin: 21.3%; Q1 2026 Frontdoor gross margin: 55%

baseline_2022.concentration: 2022 Frontdoor and First American combined share: 60.8%; Frontdoor share: 47.0%

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes mainly from annual home warranty premiums and service contract fees, plus trade call fees paid when customers request repairs, optional add-on coverage, renewals, real estate transaction-originated first-year plans, direct-to-consumer plans, builder warranties and adjacent non-warranty home services. In 2025, Frontdoor generated 76% of revenue from existing customer renewals, 7% from real estate-channel first-year warranties, 8% from direct-to-consumer first-year warranties and 9% from non-warranty and other revenue.
cost_structure: Claims and service fulfillment are the largest cost category, including payments to plumbers, HVAC contractors, electricians, appliance repair firms, replacement parts and appliances; First American reported a 40% home-warranty claim loss rate in Q2 2026, while Frontdoor reported a 55% Q1 2026 gross margin. Wages, customer service, contractor management, marketing, software, regulatory compliance and insurance/reserve costs follow. The 2022 baseline showed wages of $432 million, equal to about 11.8% of 2022 revenue, and described the model as capital-light but increasingly dependent on IT systems, self-service tools, pricing analytics and claims automation.
major_players: Frontdoor Inc. / American Home Shield / HSA / OneGuard / Landmark / 2-10 HBW
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions. Weak existing-home turnover limits real estate-channel first-year warranties, but high home values, aging systems, elevated repair costs and homeowner budget-protection demand support renewals and direct-to-consumer plans. Large operators are using price increases, contractor networks and technology to protect margins. Frontdoor’s 2025 revenue rose 14%, helped by 2-10 HBW, but its active warranty count was roughly flat at 2.11 million, showing that revenue growth is more pricing and mix-driven than unit-led. First American’s Q2 2026 home warranty revenue rose 3% year over year and pretax margin improved to 21.3%, with lower claim frequency offsetting higher claim severity.
whats_growing: Renewal revenue, price realization, builder warranty products, digital claims intake, self-service scheduling, contractor-network optimization, HVAC-related service demand, direct homeowner marketing and non-warranty home services are growing. Frontdoor expects 2026 member count to increase about 1%, first-year home warranty member count to rise about 5%, and non-warranty and other revenue to reach $220 million-$240 million.
whats_shrinking: Real estate transaction-driven demand remains pressured by high mortgage rates, affordability constraints and low existing-home turnover. Smaller regional providers face tougher competition from national brands with larger contractor networks, better pricing data and larger compliance budgets. Direct-to-consumer revenue can also be sensitive to customer acquisition costs and promotional pricing; Frontdoor expected its 2026 direct-to-consumer channel revenue to be down low single digits in its 2026 outlook.
recent_developments: 2024-12-19: Frontdoor completed its acquisition of 2-10 HBW for about $585 million, expanding into new-home builder warranties.
2025-12-31: Frontdoor reported 2025 revenue of $2.093 billion, up 14% from 2024, with approximately 2.1 million active home warranties.
2026-01-16: Forbes Home reported U.S. home warranty provider revenue of $8.87 billion in 2025, up 1.8% year over year.
2026-02-17: NAHB forecast 2026 single-family starts up 1.0% and remodeling activity up 3%, supporting repair and protection demand despite affordability headwinds.
2026-04-30: Frontdoor reported Q1 2026 revenue of $451 million, up 6%, and reaffirmed 2026 revenue guidance of $2.155 billion-$2.195 billion.
2026-07-22: First American reported Q2 2026 Home Warranty revenue of $113.8 million, up 3%, with a 21.3% pretax margin.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive. Revenue should grow faster than policy count because operators are leaning on renewal retention, 2025-2026 price increases and expanded product bundles, while high mortgage rates keep real estate-channel growth subdued. Margin resilience depends on claim frequency, HVAC and appliance replacement inflation, contractor availability and the ability to route claims digitally. Larger providers are likely to keep consolidating share because scale improves contractor access, parts purchasing, marketing efficiency and state-by-state compliance capacity. A meaningful rebound in existing-home sales would provide upside, but the base case is low- to mid-single-digit revenue growth in 2026 with continued expansion into builder warranties and broader home services.
one_sentence: In 2025-2026, the industry is growing slowly despite a weak housing transaction market because renewals, price increases, aging housing stock and adjacent home-services offerings are offsetting softer real estate-originated sales.

title: Homeopathic Medicine Manufacturing
one_liner: Small US manufacturers of homeopathic OTC remedies are growing slowly as wellness demand offsets tighter FDA and FTC scrutiny.
overview: The industry manufactures prescription and over-the-counter homeopathic remedies in forms such as pellets, tablets, creams, ointments, gels, drops and sprays. The 2022 IBIS baseline put US industry revenue at $181.9 million, profit at $15.0 million and profit margin at 8.4%. Applying the baseline 2022-2028 projected CAGR of 1.16% implies about $188.3 million in 2025 revenue and about $190.5 million in 2026 revenue. Demand is supported by consumer interest in natural and preventive health products, the 2024 US population age 65+ reaching 61.2 million, and 2024 US national health expenditure reaching $5.3 trillion, but the category remains constrained by limited clinical substantiation, conventional OTC competition and FDA/FTC enforcement expectations.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated US industry revenue: $188.3 million, inferred from the 2022 IBIS revenue base of $181.9 million and 2022-2028 projected CAGR of 1.16%.
key_stats.growth: 2022-2028 projected US industry revenue CAGR: 1.16%; 2026 estimated US industry revenue: $190.5 million using the same baseline projection.
key_stats.exports: 2022 exports: $33.7 million, equal to 18.5% of 2022 revenue.
key_stats.broader_market_context: 2025 global homeopathy product market: $11.98 billion; 2026 global forecast: $13.44 billion; 2025-2034 CAGR forecast: 12.21%; North America 2025 share: 36.0%.

baseline_2022.growth: 2017-2022 revenue CAGR: 3.7%; 2022 annual revenue change: -0.9%; 2022-2028 projected revenue CAGR: 1.16%.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers formulate, dilute, package and sell homeopathic OTC and prescription products through chain stores, mail-order/e-commerce, independent retailers, clinics and export channels. In 2022, retail channels represented 56.9% of revenue, including chain stores at 23.7% and mail service at 20.4%; exports represented 18.5%; clinics represented 13.7%; other non-retail channels represented 10.7%. Product revenue was led by cold and flu remedies at 39.8% of 2022 revenue, pain relief at 19.4%, children's medicines at 18.7% and other remedies at 22.1%.

cost_structure.labor: 2022 wages were $31.0 million, about 17.0% of 2022 revenue.
cost_structure.profit: 2022 profit was $15.0 million, about 8.4% of 2022 revenue.
cost_structure.materials_and_packaging: 2022 product mix depended on low-cost natural inputs, excipients, alcohol or water dilutions, sugar pellets, bottles, tubes, cartons and labels; exact purchase share was not disclosed in the baseline.
cost_structure.compliance_and_quality: 2025 FDA warning letters show quality testing, sterility, labeling and unapproved-drug compliance are material operating costs for homeopathic manufacturers and distributors.
cost_structure.distribution: 2022 sales relied heavily on retail and mail-service distribution, creating margin pressure from large retailers with stronger pricing power.

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions. Consumer demand for natural, preventive and self-care remedies remains favorable, helped by aging demographics and rising health spending. At the same time, FDA states that no homeopathic product is FDA-approved and has prioritized enforcement for products with safety concerns, risky routes of administration, vulnerable populations, serious-disease claims or significant quality issues. FTC health-product guidance also keeps pressure on marketers to substantiate efficacy and safety claims with competent and reliable scientific evidence. The result is slow underlying manufacturing growth, stronger scrutiny of children's, ophthalmic, injectable-like and disease-claim products, and more advantage for brands with quality systems, retail relationships and cautious labeling.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 e-commerce and mail-service availability for OTC homeopathic remedies.
2025-2026 cold, flu, allergy, respiratory and immune-support positioning within wellness retail.
2025-2026 pain-relief formats such as arnica gels, creams, sprays and tablets.
2025-2026 demand tied to older consumers, with the US age-65+ population at 61.2 million in 2024.
2025-2026 broader natural-health and complementary-care demand, with global homeopathy products estimated at $11.98 billion in 2025.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026 tolerance for unsubstantiated treatment, cure or serious-disease claims.
2025-2026 regulatory room for products marketed to children, pregnant consumers or elderly consumers without strong quality controls.
2025-2026 viability of ophthalmic, nasal, injectable-like or sterile-positioned products that fall into FDA priority enforcement categories.
2025-2026 share for small brands that cannot absorb testing, documentation, labeling and retailer-compliance requirements.
2025-2026 direct-to-consumer claims that imply FDA approval or conventional-drug equivalence.
recent_developments: 2022-12-06: FDA issued final guidance describing a risk-based enforcement approach for unapproved homeopathic drug products.
2022-12: FTC updated Health Products Compliance Guidance covering homeopathic and other health-product claims requiring scientific substantiation.
2025-08-25: FDA warned Homeopathic Educational Services over Cineraria Maritima Eye Drops marketed for cataracts as an unapproved new drug.
2025-09-16: FDA warned Stellalife over homeopathic oral-care products marketed to vulnerable populations and cited contamination concerns.
2025-10-21: FDA warned Uriel Pharmacy over homeopathic ampule drug products, CGMP issues and injection-confusion risks.
2026-07: Fortune Business Insights estimated the global homeopathy product market at $11.98 billion in 2025 and forecast $13.44 billion for 2026.
outlook: US Homeopathic Medicine Manufacturing is likely to remain a small, low-growth manufacturing niche through 2026. The 2022 IBIS projection implies revenue near $190.5 million in 2026, while the broader global product market is forecast to expand much faster from $11.98 billion in 2025 to $13.44 billion in 2026. US upside is strongest in compliant OTC formats, established retail brands, arnica pain relief, cough-cold, allergy and wellness-adjacent products. Downside risk is concentrated in unapproved serious-disease claims, products aimed at vulnerable populations, ophthalmic and injectable-like products, and manufacturers with weak CGMP documentation or inadequate ingredient and finished-product testing.

title: Homeowners' Associations in the US
one_liner: HOAs remain a growing but financially pressured housing-governance layer funded mainly by homeowner assessments.
overview: The industry is mature, fragmented and mostly nonprofit, with revenue tied to the number of association-governed homes, assessment levels, reserve funding needs and the pace of new residential development. Public 2025 data show community associations covering 35.2% of US housing, with 373,000 associations and 78.1 million residents, while 2025 industry sales were estimated at $42.2 billion. The operating story has shifted from simple membership growth to funding stress: insurance, repairs, staffing, reserve mandates and aging infrastructure are pushing boards toward higher dues, special assessments, loans, liens and stricter collections.

key_stats.housing_share: 2025: 35.2% of US housing in community associations
key_stats.homeownership_rate: 2026 Q1: 65.4% seasonally adjusted US homeownership rate
key_stats.housing_starts: 2026 June: 1.427 million privately owned housing starts at a seasonally adjusted annual rate

how_it_makes_money: Assessment fees and condo dues are the core revenue source, with the 2022 IBIS baseline putting homeowners' association and condo fees at 58.5% of revenue. Secondary revenue comes from program service fees, rental or event income, amenity fees, licensing and ticket sales for the broader NAICS category, and other member-service income. Most HOAs operate as nonprofits, so surplus is usually retained in reserves or rolled into future maintenance budgets rather than distributed as profit.
cost_structure: Major costs are property maintenance, landscaping, utilities, insurance, security, professional management, legal and accounting services, reserve contributions, repairs, capital projects and wages. The 2025 Kentley/Research and Markets listing reported 2025 operating expenses grew 3.3%, while the 2022 IBIS baseline showed wages of $7.357 billion and profit margin of 7.1%. Cost pressure is strongest in insurance-exposed coastal and wildfire markets, older condominium buildings, communities with underfunded reserves, and associations facing higher labor and contractor rates.
major_players: No dominant national HOA operator; ownership and governance are highly fragmented across nonprofit associations
FirstService Residential, Associa and RealManage are important third-party community-management firms but are not HOA owners
Large master-planned community associations in states such as Florida, California, Texas, Arizona and Nevada influence regional best practices
Community Associations Institute and the Foundation for Community Association Research are key data, training and advocacy institutions
current_dynamics: Demand is supported by the continued buildout of association-governed housing and municipal reliance on private communities to maintain roads, stormwater systems, landscaping, amenities and common areas. The 2025-2026 environment is less benign for boards: higher insurance, repair and reserve costs are colliding with affordability pressure on owners. Florida condominium reserve and inspection rules are especially influential because they force older multifamily associations to confront deferred maintenance, while national housing starts remain choppy and high mortgage rates slow turnover.
whats_growing: Association-governed housing share, third-party management demand, reserve studies, special assessments, board compliance work, digital owner portals, collections activity, insurance shopping, infrastructure planning, and demand for 55+ and amenity-rich communities are growing. The 2025 FCAR estimate of 373,000 associations and 78.1 million residents indicates continued community-count and resident expansion.
whats_shrinking: Financial flexibility is shrinking for under-reserved communities, especially older condominiums with structural, roofing, insurance or life-safety exposure. Home sales velocity and affordability-sensitive new buyer demand are weaker in high-rate markets, and volunteer board capacity is under pressure as compliance and conflict burdens rise. The 2024 IBIS public statistic showing 134,698 employees and a 2019-2024 employment CAGR of -0.3% suggests staffing growth has not kept pace with operating complexity.
recent_developments: 2024: IBISWorld reported 134,698 employees in the industry and a 2019-2024 employment CAGR of -0.3%.
2025: FCAR estimated 373,000 US community associations with 78.1 million residents and 35.2% of US housing stock in associations.
2025: CAI advocacy reported more than 900 state bills directly affecting community associations at the start of 2025.
2025: Florida condominium rules limited reserve waivers for required structural items in budgets adopted on or after December 31, 2024.
2026: Research and Markets/Kentley listed 2025 industry sales at $42.2 billion and 2020-2025 growth at 6.1% annually.
2026: US Census reported June 2026 housing starts at 1.427 million SAAR, 3.5% above June 2025.
outlook: The near-term outlook is modestly positive for revenue but tougher for affordability and governance. Market sales should keep rising as communities add homes and raise assessments, but growth will increasingly reflect cost pass-through rather than discretionary service expansion. Reserve funding, insurance availability, climate exposure and aging infrastructure will shape dues increases through 2026, while 2026 homeownership of 65.4% and uneven housing starts point to slower member growth than the post-pandemic build cycle.

title: Hops Farming
one_liner: U.S. hops farming is shrinking acreage after the craft IPA boom left the supply chain oversupplied.
overview: U.S. hops farming is a specialized agricultural industry concentrated in Washington, Idaho and Oregon, where growers produce aroma and bittering hop varieties for domestic brewers, export customers and hop merchants. After years of expansion tied to craft beer and hop-forward IPAs, the industry has been correcting since 2022: harvested acreage, production and inventories have moved down as breweries rationalize contracts and beer volumes weaken. In 2025, U.S. production fell to 83.1 million pounds and harvested acreage fell to 41,654 acres, but the value of production edged up to $447.5 million because the average price rose to $5.38 per pound.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 U.S. farm-gate value of hop production: $447.5 million
key_stats.growth: 2025 market value growth: +0.4% year over year from $445.8 million in 2024
key_stats.production: 2025 U.S. hop production: 83.1 million pounds, down 5.0% from 2024
key_stats.average_price: 2025 average price: $5.38 per pound, up from $5.12 in 2024
key_stats.stocks: March 1, 2026 hop stocks: 147.0 million pounds, down 13.0% from March 1, 2025
key_stats.2026_acres_strung: 2026 acres strung for harvest: 41,642 acres, essentially flat with 2025 harvested acreage of 41,654 acres

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 U.S. farm-gate value of hop production: $617.6 million
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 market value growth: -6.7% year over year from $661.6 million in 2021
baseline_2022.production: 2022 U.S. hop production: 101.3 million pounds, down 12.0% from 2021
baseline_2022.industry_context: The baseline IBISWorld file reported 2020 revenue of $639.6 million and projected slower growth toward 2025 as oversupply emerged.

how_it_makes_money: Growers earn revenue by selling dried whole-cone hops, pellets and contracted variety output to brewers, hop dealers and processors. Most sales are forward-contracted by variety, volume and crop year, with spot-market sales used for excess or uncovered needs. Premium aroma varieties, proprietary cultivars, organic hops and reliable quality command higher prices.

cost_structure.labor: High: trellising, training, harvest and processing require seasonal and skilled labor.
cost_structure.land_and_water: High: production is concentrated in irrigated Pacific Northwest acreage with significant water and land costs.
cost_structure.equipment_and_facilities: High: growers need trellis systems, harvesters, kilns, balers, cold storage and pelletizing or merchant relationships.
cost_structure.inputs: Moderate to high: rhizomes or plants, fertilizer, crop protection, fuel, energy and packaging are material costs.
cost_structure.selling_and_contracting: Moderate: marketing, testing, merchant fees, freight and quality assurance influence realized margins.

current_dynamics: The industry is in supply correction rather than expansion. Brewers are buying more carefully after weaker beer volumes and slower craft growth reduced hop demand, while growers have removed acreage and shifted toward clearer contract commitments. Inventories remain large relative to annual production, but 2026 stock levels show the overhang easing. Washington remains the anchor region, while Idaho and Oregon provide important variety diversity. Proprietary and high-demand aroma varieties are holding up better than legacy varieties exposed to declining mainstream and older craft recipes.
whats_growing: Demand for differentiated proprietary aroma varieties such as Citra, Mosaic, Krush and selected locally branded hops
Brewer interest in tighter contracting, traceability and quality assurance
Low- and non-alcohol beer innovation that still uses aroma hops for flavor
Organic acreage modestly rebounding in 2026, with 433 acres strung versus 409 acres harvested in 2025
whats_shrinking: Total U.S. hop production, down to 83.1 million pounds in 2025 from 101.3 million pounds in 2022
Harvested acreage, down to 41,654 acres in 2025 from 59,785 acres in 2022
Excess inventories, with March 1 stocks down to 147.0 million pounds in 2026 from 169.0 million pounds in 2025
Legacy varieties with weaker brewer pull, including continued pressure on Cascade in Washington
Distributed craft beer volume, with 2025 craft production down 4.0%
recent_developments: 2025-06-12: USDA forecast 2025 hop acres strung for harvest at 42,231 acres, down 6.0% from 2024 harvested acreage.
2025-12-19: USDA reported 2025 U.S. hop production of 83.1 million pounds, down 5.0% from 2024, with production value of $447.5 million.
2026-01-14: Brewers Association highlighted continued acreage and production declines and said the inventory overhang that peaked in 2022 had begun to reverse.
2026-03-16: USDA reported March 1, 2026 hop stocks of 147.0 million pounds, down 13.0% from March 1, 2025.
2026-04-14: Brewers Association reported 2025 craft beer production of 22.034 million barrels, down 4.0%, while overall beer volume fell 5.7%.
2026-06-12: USDA reported 2026 hop acres strung for harvest at 41,642 acres, nearly unchanged from 41,654 harvested acres in 2025.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is flat to slightly softer in volume, with acreage nearly unchanged and demand still constrained by weaker beer and craft production. Revenue should depend more on mix and price than on acreage growth: high-demand aroma varieties and well-contracted growers are better positioned, while farms exposed to spot sales or older varieties face pressure. The industry’s medium-term recovery depends on continued inventory normalization, stable brewery closures, consumer acceptance of premium beer pricing and growers’ ability to match acreage to brewer commitments.

title: Horse & Other Equine Production in the US
one_liner: A fragmented breeding-and-raising industry tied to recreational riding, show horses and racehorse economics, with 2025-2026 demand helped by premium events but pressured by a shrinking Thoroughbred foal crop, fewer race days and high care costs.
overview: The industry covers establishments primarily engaged in breeding and raising horses, mules, donkeys and other equines for racing, equestrian sport, rodeo, recreation, transportation, work and breeding stock. The baseline IBISWorld file placed 2021 revenue at $1.486 billion and projected 2021-2026 revenue growth of about 1.5% annually to just under $1.6 billion in 2026. Current 2025-2026 indicators are mixed: the wider 2023 US horse economy was large at $177 billion of total economic impact and 6.65 million horses, but the production niche remains small, fragmented and dependent on discretionary consumers, breed registries, racing purses, show entries and farm-level economics. USDA's 2022 Census counted 372,810 farms with 2,411,232 horses and ponies in inventory, while 63,018 farms sold 267,890 horses and ponies for $2.240 billion in 2022, underscoring that many equine owners are hobby, recreation or low-volume operators rather than scaled commercial producers.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: approximately $1.6 billion revenue, based on the 2022 IBISWorld baseline projection in 2021 dollars.
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026: approximately +1.5% CAGR in the baseline outlook; 2025 demand signals were softer in racing, with US Thoroughbred wagering down 2.1% and US race days down 5.2%.
key_stats.establishments: 2021: 158,095 establishments in the baseline file; 2022 USDA Census counted 372,810 farms with horses and ponies in inventory, a broader farm-count measure than IBISWorld establishments.
key_stats.employment: 2021: 163,835 workers in the baseline file; 2026 baseline outlook projected 172,298 workers.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2021: 8.1% profit margin in the baseline file, with veterinary and medical costs flagged as a 2021-2026 margin constraint.
key_stats.horse_inventory: 2022: USDA Census counted 2,411,232 horses and ponies on farms and 257,825 mules, burros and donkeys on farms.
key_stats.farm_sales: 2022: USDA Census reported 267,890 horses and ponies sold by farms for $2.240 billion, plus 28,181 mules, burros and donkeys sold for $12.6 million.
key_stats.thoroughbred_supply: 2025: The Jockey Club projected a 17,300 North American registered Thoroughbred foal crop, down 3.4% from the prior reporting point; US foal crop was estimated at 16,025 in the 2026 Fact Book.
key_stats.racing_handle: 2025: US Thoroughbred handle was nearly $11.03 billion, down 2.1% from more than $11.26 billion in 2024.
key_stats.racing_purses: 2025: US Thoroughbred purses paid were more than $1.22 billion, down 2.5% from 2024.
key_stats.wider_equine_economy: 2023: American Horse Council estimated the US horse industry added $177 billion to the economy, supported 2.2 million jobs and included 6.65 million horses.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: approximately $1.51 billion revenue, estimated by applying the baseline 2021-2027 projected CAGR of 1.45% to 2021 revenue of $1.486 billion.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: approximately +1.45% revenue growth implied by the baseline 2021-2027 projection.
baseline_2022.profit: 2021: $120 million profit and 8.1% profit margin in the baseline file; 2022 profit not separately stated in the file.
baseline_2022.domestic_demand: 2021: $1.770 billion domestic demand in the baseline file; 2022 not separately stated in the file.
baseline_2022.exports: 2021: $293 million exports in the baseline file; 2026 baseline outlook projected $320.8 million exports.
baseline_2022.imports: 2021: $577 million imports in the baseline file; 2026 baseline outlook projected $610.0 million imports.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2021: recreational horses 51.2% of revenue, racehorses 20.0%, show horses 20.0% and other horses/equines 8.8%.

how_it_makes_money: 2021: Recreational horse sales represented 51.2% of baseline industry revenue, serving riding, ranch, school, leisure and property-owner demand.
2021: Racehorses represented 20.0% of baseline industry revenue, with pricing tied to pedigrees, racing purses, auction demand and stud value.
2021: Show horses represented 20.0% of baseline industry revenue, serving dressage, jumping, rodeo, breed shows and other competitive disciplines.
2021: Other horses and equines represented 8.8% of baseline revenue, including mules, donkeys, burros and utility animals.
2025: Operators also earned revenue from stud fees, boarding, training-for-sale, foaling, transfers and registry-linked services.

cost_structure.feed_and_bedding: 2025-2026: Hay, grain, bedding and pasture costs remain a major variable expense, with alfalfa hay quoted at $195 per ton in May 2026 in USDA-sourced price data.
cost_structure.labor: 2021: Baseline wages were $225 million, and 2026 baseline employment was projected at 172,298 workers.
cost_structure.veterinary_and_health: 2026: BLS reported veterinarian services CPI up 5.1% year over year in June 2026, sustaining pressure on breeding, foaling and performance-horse care costs.
cost_structure.land_facilities_and_equipment: 2022: USDA Census reported 12.5 million acres owned or leased for horse-related purposes in the 2023 American Horse Council study, making pasture, fencing, barns, trailers and equipment structurally important costs.
cost_structure.transport_and_compliance: 2026: USDA APHIS import rules require permits, health certificates, port inspection and quarantine for most live equine imports, adding cost to international horse movement.
cost_structure.insurance_and_financing: 2025: High-value race and show horses require mortality, liability and care coverage, while small breeders face interest-rate exposure on land, barns, vehicles and equipment.

major_players: Godolphin/Darley: major 2025 US Thoroughbred breeder-owner presence, including 2025 Kentucky Derby winner Sovereignty.
Coolmore/Ashford Stud: major Kentucky-based Thoroughbred stallion and breeding operation.
Spendthrift Farm: major Kentucky Thoroughbred breeding farm and stallion operator.
WinStar Farm: major Kentucky Thoroughbred breeding, racing and sales operation.
Lane's End Farm: major Kentucky Thoroughbred breeding and sales operation.
Fragmented independent breeders, farms, ranches and studs: no single operator holds a dominant national share in 2026.
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is stable but not booming. Recreation and competition provide the largest demand base, supported by the 2023 American Horse Council estimate of 6.65 million US horses and large recreation, competition and racing economic impacts. Racing still matters because racehorse prices, stud fees and elite breeding demand are influenced by purses and media attention, but 2025 US Thoroughbred race days fell 5.2%, races fell 4.7% and handle fell 2.1%. The production side is also supply-constrained: The Jockey Club's 2025 North American registered Thoroughbred foal crop projection of 17,300 was down 3.4%, and the 2026 Fact Book estimated the 2025 US foal crop at 16,025. Cost pressure remains material, with 2026 veterinary services inflation and 2026 hay prices directly affecting breeder margins.
whats_growing: 2023: Recreation generated $36.7 billion of total US horse-industry impact, the largest segment in the American Horse Council sector split.
2023: Competition generated $37.3 billion of total US horse-industry impact, supporting ongoing demand for trained show and sport horses.
2025: Kentucky Derby all-sources wagering set records at $349.0 million for Derby Day, $234.4 million for the Derby race and $473.9 million for Derby Week.
2025: AQHA reported 90,986 registrations and 785,903 total show entries for 2024, showing continued scale in the Quarter Horse registry and show ecosystem.
2026: Digital competition tools and online registry workflows are expanding, including USEF's 2026 EZ Entry pilot and AQHA's 2025 revamped online registration system.
whats_shrinking: 2025: US Thoroughbred wagering fell 2.1% to nearly $11.03 billion from more than $11.26 billion in 2024.
2025: US Thoroughbred race days fell 5.2% to 3,590, and races fell 4.7% to 29,401.
2025: US Thoroughbred purses paid fell 2.5% to more than $1.22 billion.
2025: The Jockey Club projected the North American registered Thoroughbred foal crop at 17,300, down 3.4% from the prior reporting point.
2022: USDA Census showed the broader US farm count fell to 1,900,487 farms, down 7.0% from 2017, reinforcing consolidation pressure around small agricultural operations.
recent_developments: 2024-02-13: USDA released 2022 Census data showing 372,810 farms with 2,411,232 horses and ponies in inventory and 63,018 farms selling 267,890 horses and ponies for $2.240 billion.
2025-05-03: Churchill Downs reported record 2025 Kentucky Derby wagering of $349.0 million on Derby Day, $234.4 million on the Derby race and $473.9 million for Derby Week.
2025-10-21: The Jockey Club projected a 2025 North American registered Thoroughbred foal crop of 17,300, down 3.4%, with 1,099 stallions covering 27,180 mares in 2024.
2025-11-20: EDCC began tracking a multi-state 2025 EHV-1/EHM outbreak linked to November 2025 barrel racing and rodeo events, raising biosecurity costs and event-risk awareness.
2026-01-05: Equibase reported 2025 US Thoroughbred handle down 2.1%, race days down 5.2% and races down 4.7%.
2026-03-24: HISA reported 2025 racetracks under HISA rules recorded 1.04 racing-related equine fatalities per 1,000 starts, continuing post-HISA safety gains.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is slow-growth and margin-sensitive. The baseline 2021-2026 path to roughly $1.6 billion remains plausible, but 2025 racing data argue against a sharp acceleration in racehorse demand. Recreational and competition buyers should continue to support the largest share of production revenue, especially in states with deep horse ownership and show ecosystems, while elite bloodstock prices remain tied to auction confidence, purses and stallion demand. Cost inflation in veterinary care, feed, labor, insurance and transport will limit profit expansion. Biosecurity and welfare regulation are likely to become more important operating requirements after the 2025 EHV-1/EHM outbreak and HISA's ongoing 2025-2026 safety reporting. The strongest producers in 2026 will be those with recognized bloodlines, diversified boarding/training income, direct buyer relationships and disciplined herd-size management.
